judgments.reasoning_cat1: The preamble is a plain identification of two individual Consultants, a Georgia LLC Company, and an effective date keyed to last signature, with no vague operative term to construe; the only softness is that it defines a joint plural term ("Consultants") without saying whether they hold rights jointly or severally. The signature block shows different dates, but the last-signed rule itself is mechanically determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.a pays "Consultant" in the singular while the preamble defines the collective "Consultants," and Section 2.b uses the plural again, so the definition sits awkwardly against the payment provisions on whether 20% is shared or owed to each. That mismatch is real but is naturally litigated at Section 2 rather than in the preamble itself.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The recitals contain several unbounded phrases — "long-term investment," reliance on a port "scheduled for construction in 2023," and services "to enhance the value for the sale of the property" — none of which has an applicable boundary. The clause also mixes past assistance with a future, request-contingent service obligation, leaving unclear whether any performance is promised.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The recital frames the payment as compensation "for their consulting services" rendered on request, whereas operative Sections 2.a and 2.b make the 20% payable simply upon a sale or on realized tax savings with no service condition — a classic recital-versus-operative divergence. Section 3's integration clause also invites argument over whether these Whereas clauses can qualify Section 2 at all.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Profit" is defined by subtracting "reasonable expenses, holding costs and expenses relating to transactions regarding the property (i.e. donations, etc)" — "reasonable," "holding costs" and the misused "i.e." followed by "etc" leave the deduction categories and the catch-all's reach genuinely open. This is both lexical vagueness and a general-versus-specific list problem in a single sentence.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with Section 2.b, the same 100-acre donation appears both as a deductible "expense relating to transactions" reducing Profit and as an independent source of tax savings the Consultants share, which is hard to harmonise. Applying the definition to a partial sale under Section 2.a (allocating holding costs to "a portion") also strains the whole instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Upon sale of a portion or all of Delta Bluffs" does not say how Profit is computed for a partial sale or whether expenses are allocated pro rata, and it says "pay Consultant" in the singular for two named payees. It also fixes no time for payment beyond "upon sale."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its operation depends entirely on the Section 1 Profit definition, whose "reasonable expenses" and donation carve-out control the amount, and the singular "Consultant" conflicts with the preamble's plural definition and with Section 2.b's "Consultants." Whether the recital's request-based service condition qualifies this unconditional obligation is a further whole-instrument question.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sentence is a comma splice joining a permissive statement ("may realize certain tax savings") to an obligation, and "its principal," "such savings," and "once the risk of a federal or state tax audit has expired, which is expected to occur in October 2016" each admit competing readings — notably whether October 2016 is the trigger or a mere estimate. "Certain tax savings" is undefined and unquantified.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Tax savings are labelled "Profits from Tax Savings" yet Section 1 defines Profit only as sale proceeds less expenses, so the defined term does not fit this subsection; the donation also features in Section 1 as a deductible expense and in the recital as work already performed. Payment measured by savings realized by "its principal" rather than by the contracting Company sits uneasily with the preamble's party definition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is limited to the entire agreement "in connection with Delta Bluffs," a subject-matter qualifier that leaves other dealings between these parties outside it, and the sentence ends in a comma as though truncated. It also lacks any no-oral-modification or reliance-disclaimer language, so its effect on extrinsic evidence is arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be squared with the recitals' references to the relied-upon appraisal, the prior donation and the promise of future services on request — matters the operative sections do not address — raising whether those understandings survive or are superseded. Nothing else in this three-section instrument directly contradicts it, so the tension is interpretive rather than a flat conflict.
